text:
<meta>continues from previous page: Ping'er is describing the injuries sustained by Jia Lian after he was beaten by his father, Jia She.</meta>

"...used the boards and sticks. He just stood there, and I do not know what they hit him with, but they gave him a beating, and his face was cut in two places. We heard that the Mistress <note>Madam Xue, Baochai’s mother</note> has a medicine here for wounds from a beating; could you find a pill for me, Miss?"

Baochai, hearing this, quickly ordered Ying'er to find two pills to give to Ping'er. Baochai said: "Since that is the case, go and send my regards on my behalf; I will not go there myself." Ping'er gave her word to Baochai and left. We shall say no more of this.

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her dinner, and while Baochai and the others had gone to see the Matriarch <note>Grandmother Jia</note>, she went to the <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Nightingale’s Pavilion</gloss>. By this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also come into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling said with a smile: "Now that I have come in and have some free time, if you would only teach me how to write poetry, it would be my great good fortune!"

Daiyu smiled and said: "Since you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not fully proficient, I can at least teach you the basics." 

Xiangling laughed: "If that is truly the case, I will acknowledge you as my teacher. You must not find me tiresome."

Daiyu said: "What is so difficult about it that it is worth specifically 'learning'? It is nothing more than the <term>qi-cheng-zhuan-he</term> <gloss>opening, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. The middle 'development' and 'transition' are simply two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, 'empty' words against 'solid' words, and 'solid' against 'empty'. If one truly has a remarkable line, one can even use it without worrying if the tones or word-types match perfectly."

Xiangling laughed: "No wonder I often used to secretly look at a few poems in an old book; some matched perfectly while others did not. I also heard people say, 'One, three, and five do not matter; two, four, and six must be distinct' <note>original: "一三五不論，二四六分明", a rule referring to the tonal requirements of specific positions in a line of Chinese regulated verse</note>. When looking at the poems of the ancients, some followed this, but some were wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. So I was confused every day. Now that I hear you say it, it turns out these rules do not matter as long as the phrasing is novel and extraordinary."

Daiyu said: "That is exactly the point. Phrasing is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the intent. If the poetic intent and interest are genuine, then the poem is naturally good even without polished phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words damage the intent' <note>original: "不為辭害意"</note>."

Xiangling said: "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>the poet Lu You</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the old inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' I find them so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu said: "Because you do not yet know poetry, you love these shallow and accessible lines. Once you enter into that pattern, you will never be able to learn your way out. Just listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the <term>Wang Mo-jie Quanji</term> <gloss>Complete Works of Wang Wei</gloss> here. Take a hundred of his five-character regulated poems and study them until you have thoroughly grasped them. Then, read one hundred and twenty of 'Old Du’s' <note>the poet Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems. After that, read one or two hundred of Li Qing-lian’s <note>the poet Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three poets as your foundation, you can look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. Since you are such a clever and sharp person, in less than a year’s time, you need not worry about not becoming a poet!"

Hearing this, Xiangling smiled and said: "In that case, dear Miss, please bring that book out for me. I will take it back and it will be good to read a few poems at night." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of Wang the Right Prime Minister <note>the poet Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying: "Only look at the ones with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Althea Court</gloss>. Ignoring all other matters, she simply began to read the poems one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her so dedicated, Baochai had no choice but to leave her to it.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling approaching with a beaming face to return the book and request the poems of Du Fu. Daiyu smiled and asked: "How many of them do you remember?"

Xiangling smiled: "I have read all of those marked with red circles."

Daiyu asked: "Have you gained any understanding from them?"

Xiangling laughed: "I have indeed grasped something, but I do not know if it is right. Let me tell it to you."

<summary>Xiangling begins her education in classical poetry under Lin Daiyu, who emphasizes that poetic intent and original thought are more important than rigid formal rules. Daiyu provides a structured reading list of Tang dynasty masters, and Xiangling displays immediate and intense devotion to her studies.</summary>
<keywords>Xiangling, Lin Daiyu, poetry education, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, poetic intent, regulated verse, Prospect Garden, literary criticism</keywords>
